questions.question: A graph has non-negative edge weights of varying sizes. Which algorithm is the standard choice for single-source shortest paths?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra with a priority queue runs in O((V + E) log V) and is correct for non-negative weights. BFS only handles equal weights; Bellman-Ford works but is slower at O(V x E).

questions.question: In the lazy-deletion version of Dijkstra, what does the check `if (d > dist.get(node)) continue;` do?
options: Skips heap entries that are outdated because a shorter distance to that node was found later
Stops the algorithm once the target is reached
Prevents nodes with zero-weight edges from being processed
questions.explanation: The heap cannot decrease a key, so a new entry is pushed whenever a distance improves. Older entries for the same node carry larger distances and are ignored when popped.

questions.question: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle?
options: It finds a node with no outgoing edges
The heap becomes empty before all nodes are visited
A node is visited twice during DFS
After V - 1 rounds of relaxation, some edge can still reduce a distance
questions.explanation: Without negative cycles, all shortest paths use at most V - 1 edges and are settled after V - 1 rounds. If an extra pass still improves a distance, a negative cycle is reachable.

questions.question: In the cheapest-flight-with-at-most-K-stops problem, why does each Bellman-Ford round copy the cost array?
options: So each round extends paths by exactly one edge, respecting the stop limit
Because JavaScript arrays cannot be updated inside a for...of loop
To make the algorithm run in O(V + E)
questions.explanation: Reading from the previous round's array and writing to a new one means a single round cannot chain several flights. K stops means at most K + 1 edges, so K + 1 rounds give the correct answer.
